note: Cards are PATTERNS, not problems. Scheduling individual problems trains recall of those problems; scheduling the recognition cue generalizes. `cue` is the highest-value field -- in an interview you need to know what to reach for within 60 seconds, not to have memorized a solution.

cards.name: Two pointers
cards.cue: Sorted array (or sortable) and you need a pair/triple meeting a condition. Also: comparing from both ends, or partitioning in place.
cards.invariant: Every step provably eliminates one candidate from consideration, so O(n) replaces O(n^2).
cards.trap: Reaching for it on unsorted input where sorting destroys required index order. Return indices before sorting, or use a hashmap instead.
problems: Remove Duplicates from Sorted Array II

cards.name: Sliding window
cards.cue: Contiguous subarray/substring, and asking for longest/shortest/count satisfying a constraint that is monotonic as the window grows.
cards.invariant: The window only ever moves right; each element enters and leaves once, so O(n).
cards.trap: Applying it when the constraint is not monotonic (e.g. 'subarray sum equals k' with negative numbers -- shrinking may re-satisfy it). Use prefix sums there.

cards.name: Monotonic stack
cards.cue: 'Next greater / previous smaller' for every element, or a histogram-shaped problem.
cards.invariant: The stack holds indices whose answer is still unresolved, in monotone order. An element is popped exactly when its answer is found.
cards.trap: Storing values instead of indices when the answer needs a distance. Also forgetting to drain the stack at the end.

cards.name: Binary search on the answer
cards.cue: Asking to minimize a maximum (or maximize a minimum), and you can cheaply CHECK whether a candidate answer is feasible.
cards.invariant: feasible(x) is monotone in x, so the answer space is sorted even when the input is not.
cards.trap: Not proving monotonicity of the predicate first -- this is the whole technique, and it fails silently if the predicate is not monotone.
problems: Capacity To Ship Packages Within D Days
Minimize Max Distance to Gas Station

cards.name: Prefix sum + hashmap
cards.cue: Count or find subarrays summing to k, especially with negatives (where sliding window fails).
cards.invariant: sum(i..j) == prefix[j] - prefix[i-1]; store counts of seen prefixes to find complements in O(1).
cards.trap: Forgetting to seed the map with {0: 1} for subarrays starting at index 0.

cards.name: Union-Find (DSU)
cards.cue: Dynamic connectivity, grouping, or 'are these two in the same component' with edges arriving over time.
cards.invariant: Path compression + union by rank gives near-O(1) amortized (inverse Ackermann).
cards.trap: Using it when you need to REMOVE edges -- DSU is add-only. Process offline in reverse if the problem deletes.

cards.name: Topological sort
cards.cue: Dependencies, ordering, prerequisites, or detecting a cycle in a directed graph.
cards.invariant: Kahn's: repeatedly emit a node with in-degree 0. If fewer than n emitted, a cycle exists.
cards.trap: Using DFS-based toposort and forgetting the three-color state -- 'visited' alone cannot distinguish a back edge from a cross edge.

cards.name: Dijkstra / weighted shortest path
cards.cue: Shortest path with non-negative weights. Also: 'minimize the maximum edge' variants with a modified relaxation.
cards.invariant: Once popped from the heap, a node's distance is final -- which is exactly what negative weights break.
cards.trap: Negative edges (use Bellman-Ford). Also: not skipping stale heap entries, which turns it quadratic.

cards.name: BFS on implicit graphs
cards.cue: Shortest number of steps where each move costs 1, and states are generated rather than stored (word ladders, board states, lock combinations).
cards.invariant: BFS visits states in nondecreasing distance, so the first time you reach a state is optimal.
cards.trap: Marking visited on dequeue rather than enqueue -- this admits duplicates and can blow up exponentially.

cards.name: DP over subsequences
cards.cue: Two sequences and an edit/match/align question, or one sequence with 'pick a subset in order'.
cards.invariant: dp[i][j] answers the prefix pair (i, j); the recurrence branches on whether the current elements are used.
cards.trap: Getting the base row/column wrong. Write out the n=0 and n=1 cases explicitly before coding.

cards.name: Interval DP
cards.cue: Answer for a range depends on splitting it at some k -- merging stones, bursting balloons, matrix chains.
cards.invariant: dp[i][j] = best over k in (i,j) of dp[i][k] + dp[k][j] + cost. Iterate by increasing length.
cards.trap: Iterating i and j in the natural order instead of by interval LENGTH, so subproblems are not yet computed.

cards.name: Knapsack family
cards.cue: Choose items under a capacity/budget to optimize a value, or count ways to hit a target.
cards.invariant: 0/1 iterates capacity DESCENDING (each item once); unbounded iterates ASCENDING (reuse allowed).
cards.trap: The loop direction. Getting it backwards silently converts one problem into the other.

cards.name: Backtracking with pruning
cards.cue: Enumerate all valid configurations; the search space is exponential but constraints cut it hard.
cards.invariant: Undo state on the way out; prune the moment a partial solution cannot be completed.
cards.trap: Duplicate results from unsorted input with repeats. Sort first, then skip i > start && a[i] == a[i-1].

cards.name: Heap / top-k
cards.cue: k-th largest, k closest, merge k sorted things, or a running median.
cards.invariant: A size-k min-heap keeps the k largest in O(n log k) -- smaller and faster than sorting everything.
cards.trap: Using a max-heap of size n when a min-heap of size k suffices. For running median, two heaps with a size invariant.
problems: Kth Largest Element in an Array

cards.name: Trie
cards.cue: Prefix queries, autocomplete, or matching many patterns against one text.
cards.invariant: Path from root spells a prefix; shared prefixes cost nothing extra.
cards.trap: Building a trie when a hashmap of full strings would do -- only worth it when PREFIXES are queried.

cards.name: Fast/slow pointers
cards.cue: Cycle detection, finding a midpoint, or the k-th from the end in one pass with O(1) space.
cards.invariant: Floyd: if a cycle exists the pointers meet; restarting one at head and stepping both by 1 finds the entry.
cards.trap: Off-by-one on the midpoint -- decide up front whether you want the first or second middle for even length.

cards.name: Interval merging / sweep line
cards.cue: Overlapping ranges: merge, count max concurrent, insert, or find free gaps.
cards.invariant: Sort by start (or split into +1/-1 events and sort by time); a single pass then suffices.
cards.trap: Tie-breaking when an interval ends exactly where another starts. Decide whether touching counts as overlapping and encode it in the sort.

cards.name: Bit manipulation
cards.cue: Small fixed universe (<= 20-ish elements) for subset enumeration, XOR tricks, or counting set bits.
cards.invariant: x & (x-1) clears the lowest set bit; XOR is its own inverse and cancels pairs.
cards.trap: Signed shifts and overflow in languages without arbitrary precision. In Python, watch for unbounded ints in mask loops.
problems: Minimum Number of K Consecutive Bit Flips

cards.name: Greedy with an exchange argument
cards.cue: Local choice looks optimal and you can argue any optimal solution can be transformed into the greedy one without getting worse.
cards.invariant: The exchange argument IS the proof. Without it, greedy is a guess.
cards.trap: Asserting greedy works because it passes the examples. Interviewers probe exactly here -- have the argument ready.

cards.name: String matching (KMP / rolling hash)
cards.cue: Substring search, periodicity, or comparing many substrings in O(1).
cards.invariant: KMP's failure function = longest proper prefix that is also a suffix. Rolling hash gives O(1) substring compare with collision risk.
cards.trap: Rolling hash with a weak modulus -- use a large prime and ideally double hashing. Interviewers will ask about collisions.

cards.name: Segment tree / Fenwick
cards.cue: Range queries WITH point or range updates interleaved. Prefix sums alone fail once updates appear.
cards.invariant: O(log n) per query and update; Fenwick is smaller/faster but only for invertible operations.
cards.trap: Reaching for it when the array is static -- prefix sums are simpler and faster. Only justified when updates interleave.
problems: Count of Smaller Numbers After Self

cards.name: Grid traversal / flood fill
cards.cue: 2D grid with regions, islands, or distance-from-multiple-sources.
cards.invariant: Multi-source BFS: push all sources at distance 0, then a single BFS gives distance-to-nearest for every cell.
cards.trap: Running BFS once per source (quadratic) when multi-source in one pass is linear.
